sysd-blocks-139.title: Memory versus storage: how a computer keeps its bits
sysd-blocks-139.text: Every text, number, image and sound a computer holds is a string of bits. Computer data storage is the retention of digital data using computer components and recording media, and its most common unit is the byte, equal to 8 bits. Two words are easy to confuse. Faster, volatile components are generally called memory, while slower, persistent ones are called storage. In current usage, storage means devices the CPU cannot reach directly, and memory means semiconductor read-write storage, typically DRAM. Keeping data brings choices. Compression uses a shorter bit string and takes tens of percent less storage for many kinds of data, but it costs more computation and may delay access. Encryption keeps chunks of stored snapshots from being rebuilt without permission. Check data and extra copies let a computer detect a random bit flip and correct it, through disk mirroring or {{ref:sysd-blocks-149}}. Every medium also fails in its own way: head crashes on mechanical hard drives and electronic faults in flash can cause instant total loss.

sysd-blocks-199.title: Hard disk drives: waiting for the platter to come around
sysd-blocks-199.text: At 7,200 rpm, a hard disk waits 4.16 ms on average for the right sector to spin under the head; at 5,400 rpm the wait is 5.55 ms. A hard disk drive (HDD) is an electro-mechanical device that stores digital data magnetically on rapidly rotating platters. Magnetic heads on a moving actuator arm read and write them, in any order, and the data persists when power is off. Mechanics limit access time: seek time to move the head to the right track, rotational latency, and the time to transfer the data. Access time has not kept up with throughput, which has not kept up with the growth in bit density and capacity. HDDs cost much less per bit than the drives of {{ref:sysd-blocks-195}}, which cost four to nine times more, and HDDs still dominate the volume of server storage produced. Each block carries error-correcting bits, so a typical 1 TB disk with 512-byte sectors spends about 93 GB on them. Because single drives fail, storage providers rely on redundant HDD arrays and replace failed drives continually.

sysd-blocks-192.title: Volatile memory: fast, and forgetful without power
sysd-blocks-192.text: Cut the power and volatile memory forgets everything, quickly. It needs power to keep its contents, and most general-purpose random-access memory (RAM) is volatile. It serves as primary storage, a role {{ref:sysd-blocks-140}} explains. It is usually faster than mass storage such as a hard disk drive, and its forgetfulness has a use: sensitive information becomes unavailable on power-down. There are two kinds, and both need continuous electrical current. Dynamic RAM (DRAM) keeps each bit in a capacitor and needs only one capacitor and one transistor per bit, so it is space-efficient, inexpensive and very popular. Static RAM (SRAM) is much faster and needs no refreshes, but each bit takes a cell of six transistors, so it cannot reach DRAM's capacity. SRAM is commonly used as CPU cache, for processor registers and in networking devices.

sysd-blocks-193.title: Non-volatile memory: data that outlives the power
sysd-blocks-193.text:
Pull the plug and some memory still remembers. Non-volatile memory retains stored information even after power is removed, which is why it is typically used for secondary storage or long-term persistent storage. Most forms are unsuitable as primary storage, because compared with volatile RAM they typically cost more, perform worse or have a limited lifetime.

The family splits by how a location is reached. Electrically addressed memory, such as {{ref:sysd-blocks-194}} and read-only memory, is generally expensive and limited in capacity but fast. Mechanically addressed memory, such as hard disks, optical discs, magnetic tape and holographic memory, costs less per bit but is slower. These use a recording head: tape is sequential, since it must pass the head, while hard disks and optical discs give random access.

Read-only memory comes in grades. Mask ROMs are programmed only at the factory, and PROM can be written once. EPROM is erasable by ultraviolet light but clears the whole device at once. EEPROM erases with voltage, but slowly. Newer electrically addressed technologies include ferroelectric RAM, magnetoresistive RAM, phase-change memory and ReRAM. ReRAM was seen as a flash replacement, but its cost and performance benefits have not persuaded companies to switch. Non-volatile main memory, NVDIMM being one example, is primary storage with non-volatile attributes, and it presents security challenges.

sysd-blocks-210.title: Durability: a commit that survives the crash
sysd-blocks-210.text: A database says the transaction is committed, and then the machine crashes. Durability is the ACID guarantee that the effects of committed transactions survive permanently, even through failures and catastrophic events. A durable system must survive three kinds of failure. Transaction failures interrupt a transaction. System failures lose volatile storage in a crash. Media failures lose stable storage, typically a disk. Whatever happens, the changes of incomplete transactions are reverted. To survive the loss of volatile memory, the database flushes an immutable sequential log of transactions to non-volatile storage before acknowledging a commit. This is the write-ahead log. Because changes are logged before they modify database state, committed transactions can be redone from it after a crash, and incomplete ones undone. Against media failure, stable memory is built from copying and robust writing protocols such as disk mirroring. Offline copies, checkpoints, incremental dumps and differential files save space and time compared with replaying every log file from the start. In a distributed database all nodes must coordinate before a commit is acknowledged, usually by {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}.

sysd-blocks-140.title: The storage hierarchy: from nanoseconds to robot arms
sysd-blocks-140.text:
Some data a computer reaches in nanoseconds. Other data takes 5 to 60 seconds, because a robot has to fetch it. The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage.

Primary storage, or main memory, holds the instructions the CPU continuously reads and the data it is actively using. Secondary storage is not directly accessible by the CPU, so input/output channels transfer the desired data into primary storage. It is non-volatile and usually an HDD or SSD, with access time per byte in milliseconds against nanoseconds for primary storage. It is less expensive, so modern systems typically have two orders of magnitude more of it. It is addressable by block and moved in large contiguous blocks to reduce seek time and rotational latency. Using several disks in parallel, as in {{ref:sysd-blocks-149}}, increases the bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and eases the I/O bottleneck.

Tertiary storage uses a robotic arm to mount removable media. It suits archiving rarely accessed data in extraordinarily large stores, but it is much slower than secondary storage: 5 to 60 seconds against 1 to 10 milliseconds. Offline storage sits on media that are removed or disconnected, and unlike tertiary storage it cannot be accessed without human interaction.

sysd-blocks-194.title: Flash memory: NOR for random reads, NAND for bulk
sysd-blocks-194.text: Flash memory is a solid-state chip that maintains stored data without any external power source. It is a close relative of EEPROM, but erase operations must be done on a block basis and its capacity is substantially larger. Two designs dominate. NOR flash gives high-speed random access, reading and writing specific locations, and can retrieve as little as a single byte. NAND flash reads and writes sequentially at high speed in blocks and reads faster than it writes, though it is slower at reading than NOR. At high densities NAND costs less and offers more capacity for the same silicon. NAND cells are classed by bits per cell. Single-level cells hold 1 bit and give the best performance and endurance, at higher cost. MLC, TLC and QLC cells hold 2, 3 and 4 bits, cost less, and perform and endure less. Many drives, such as those in {{ref:sysd-blocks-195}}, use 3D NAND, with cells stacked vertically, which raises density while improving performance and reducing costs.

sysd-blocks-195.title: Solid-state drives: no moving parts, new ways to fail
sysd-blocks-195.text: A random read on a consumer NAND solid-state drive typically takes 0.05 to 0.2 ms. On a high-end hard disk it takes 2.9 ms, and on a laptop one 12 ms. A solid-state drive (SSD) uses integrated circuits, typically NAND flash, to store data persistently. With no moving parts it offers lower latency, resistance to physical shock, lower power consumption and silent operation. The price: SSDs are generally more expensive per gigabyte and have a finite number of write cycles, while hard disks offer far more capacity for the money. Every SSD has a controller, an embedded processor running firmware that manages data flow between the NAND and the host. It does bad block mapping, ECC, garbage collection, wear leveling, caching and encryption. SSDs also fail differently: sudden power loss can leave incomplete writes, and one failed chip can lose all data on it. Studies find lower failure rates than HDDs but more uncorrectable errors, and firmware bugs are a major cause of data loss.

sysd-blocks-200.title: How hard disks fail, and how drives hide it
sysd-blocks-200.text: The dramatic failure is the head crash: the head scrapes the platter and grinds away its magnetic film. Quieter faults the drive hides itself, remapping a failing sector's data to a spare while error correction can still recover it. S.M.A.R.T. counts those fixes but warns only of mechanical issues. Uncorrected bit read errors are specified at one in 10^16 bits for 2013 enterprise drives and one in 10^14 for 2018 consumer drives. Silent corruption is the worst kind. Drive grade does not predict failure rate, failure rates rise steadily with age, and in an array one drive's failure significantly raises the short-term risk of a second.

sysd-blocks-201.title: How drives connect: SATA, SAS, PCIe and NVMe
sysd-blocks-201.text: A fast drive on a slow connection is still slow. Hard drives connect over parallel ATA, Serial ATA (SATA), SCSI, Serial Attached SCSI (SAS) or {{ref:sysd-blocks-207}}. SAS is a serial protocol that still uses SCSI commands. It is compatible with SATA: a SAS controller can drive SATA drives, but a SATA controller cannot drive SAS drives. SSDs use SATA 3.0 at up to 6.0 Gbit/s, SAS 3.0 at 12.0 Gbit/s or PCIe 3.0 x4 at 31.5 Gbit/s. NVMe, built for SSDs, offers much lower latency and higher throughput than AHCI.

sysd-blocks-141.title: Telling storage technologies apart
sysd-blocks-141.text: Two storage devices can look alike and behave nothing alike. Technologies are told apart by volatility, mutability, accessibility, addressability, capacity and density, and performance. Accessibility comes in two modes. In random access, any location is reached in about the same time. In sequential access, pieces are read in serial order, so access time depends on which piece was read last. Storage can also be location accessible, selected by numerical memory address, file addressable, or content-addressable. Performance is measured by latency, throughput, granularity and reliability.

sysd-blocks-143.title: Block storage: raw blocks owned by one server
sysd-blocks-143.text: A database would rather have the raw disk than a tidy folder tree. Block storage gives it that. It divides data into blocks and stores them as separate pieces, each with a unique identifier, and presents the raw blocks to the server as a volume. A volume is a fixed amount of storage on a disk or tape. The server can format it as a file system or hand control of the blocks to an application. That makes block storage the most flexible and versatile form, and databases manage blocks directly to squeeze out the most performance. The identifiers let the system place pieces wherever is most convenient and reassemble them on request. Disks attached to a server, hard or solid-state, are all block storage. It can also be reached over a high-speed network, through protocols such as {{ref:sysd-blocks-207}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-206}}. Even then it presents raw blocks and is fully owned by one server, not a shared resource. In the cloud it emulates a physical block device such as a hard drive; Amazon EBS is an example.

sysd-blocks-149.title: RAID: many drives acting as one safer drive
sysd-blocks-149.text: Add drives to a machine and failures grow more frequent. Yet an array of drives can be far more reliable than any single high-capacity drive, and RAID is how. RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) stores the same data on several hard disks or SSDs, so data survives a drive failure. Not every RAID level aims at that. RAID coordinates two or more drives into a disk array and distributes written data across it. The configurations are called {{ref:sysd-blocks-150}}. They differ in how much extra data they keep, how many drives they need, how fast they run, and how many failures they survive. The defining techniques are data striping, to improve read and write efficiency, and disk mirroring or parity drives, for data recovery. Using several disks in parallel also increases the bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and eases the I/O bottleneck. RAID guards against physical drive failure only. Operator error, software, hardware and virus destruction still threaten the data, and fire can take the whole array, so extra copies can be stored off site.

sysd-blocks-206.title: iSCSI: disk commands carried over ordinary IP networks
sysd-blocks-206.text: iSCSI lets a database server believe a remote disk is plugged in next to it. It is an IP-based storage networking standard that provides block-level access to storage devices by carrying SCSI commands over a TCP/IP network. Clients, called initiators, send commands to storage devices, called targets, on remote servers. A LUN (logical unit number) is an individually addressable logical SCSI device within a target, essentially a numbered disk. Initiators treat LUNs like raw disks. Rather than mounting remote directories as with {{ref:sysd-blocks-202}}, the host formats and manages a file system on the LUN. It needs no dedicated cabling and runs over existing IP infrastructure, so it is seen as a low-cost alternative to {{ref:sysd-blocks-207}}. The catch is competition for a fixed amount of bandwidth. A storage network can be severely degraded if it does not run on a dedicated network or VLAN. It mostly sends cleartext over TCP, so administrators usually isolate it on logically separate networks and authenticate initiators and targets with CHAP. It also serves storage consolidation: a server gets a new disk volume without cabling changes.

sysd-blocks-155.title: Data scrubbing: finding bad blocks before you need them
sysd-blocks-155.text: A block nobody reads can go bad unnoticed. Data scrubbing, also called patrol read, has the RAID controller periodically read and check every block in an array. That includes blocks not otherwise accessed, so bad blocks are detected before use. It uses the array's extra data to recover a bad block on a single drive and reassigns the recovered data to spare blocks elsewhere on the drive. Run as a background process, scrubbing finds and recovers from unrecoverable read errors, which reduces the risk of them causing double-drive failures during a rebuild.

sysd-blocks-156.title: Hardware or software: where RAID logic lives
sysd-blocks-156.text: Somebody has to decide which drive gets which piece of data. That job can sit in dedicated hardware. It can also sit in software, in the operating system or in the firmware and drivers of a standard drive controller. Hardware RAID controllers are expensive and proprietary, and each manufacturer's tooling for each operating system ensures vendor lock-in. Many modern operating systems provide software RAID. It may be a device-abstraction layer such as Linux md, a logical volume manager such as LVM, or a file system component such as ZFS or Btrfs. Cheaper firmware- and driver-based controllers may not work when the host operating system lacks driver support.
